newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AIOC Caspian oil group pushes back startup date.
newsitem.headline: AIOC Caspian oil group pushes back startup date.

text.p: The $8 billion Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC) oil consortium said on Monday it had pushed back its production start-up date by about a month to the end of September.

The group, led by a British Petroleum -Statoil alliance, had originally planned to start output on August 28. But it said bureaucratic delays and bad weather had pushed the date back to the end of September.

"Now that the picture is clearer, it appears we will have the first wellhead production from the (Chirag-1) platform in the latter part of September," said Tamam Bayatly, an AIOC spokeswoman in the Azeri capital of Baku.

Bayatly said the group received intergovernmental sanctions to start up production later than it had expected, and the weather around Baku had been unusually bad last winter. But she played down the commercial significance of the delays.

"We are not that much behind (the original schedule)," Bayatly said. "A couple of weeks here or there is not a great difference, and we still consider it an outstanding achievement to have first oil by late September."

The group expects to produce between 40,000 and 50,000 tonnes of oil in 1997, rising to 1.5 million (30,000 barrels per day) in 1998, Bayatly said. The consortium forecasts peak output at 700,000 to 800,000 bpd by 2007-2010.

Bayatly said the first production well was drilled at the Chirag-1 platform last week, and the drilling would take 45 days to complete. Another production well is slated for the same platform, although the timing is undecided.
"Within three years we are planning 24 wells from that platform," she said.
AIOC is developing three major oil deposits -- Chirag, Azeri and deep-water Gyuneshli -- which Azerbaijan says lie in its territory of the Caspian Sea.
Reserves of recoverable energy in the contract area containing the three fields are pegged at 550 million tonnes of oil and 82 billion cubic feet of natural gas.
AIOC needs the so-called northern oil export route, linking Baku with Russia's Black Sea export outlet of Novorossiisk, ready by the end of 1998 to get its oil to world markets.

The route crosses the independence-minded Russian republic of Chechnya, and talks between Chechen oil company YUNKO and Russian oil pipeline monopoly Transneft have so far failed to yield an agreement.

AIOC needs the pipeline to be ready by end-1998 to export its early oil. A second existing pipeline, known as the western route linking Baku with the Georgian Black Sea port of Batumi, is not due to be ready for use until end-1998.
AIOC is watching the YUNKO-Transneft talks closely for signs of a breakthrough in the thorny issue of tariffs.

Also key for the oil transport deal are political relations between Moscow and Grozny. Russian President Boris Yeltsin met Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov in the Kremlin on Monday, but politics, not oil dominated the talks.
Azeri state oil firm SOCAR, also a part of the AIOC consortium, has agreed with Transneft to use the route even earlier -- by October 1.
The route across Chechnya will take around one month to repair once a deal has been signed, leaving little room for manoeuvre, particularly from SOCAR's point of view.
AIOC is hopeful Transneft can honour its deal to carry SOCAR oil, as this would clear the way for exports of its early oil.
"We have to believe in what Transneft has undertaken with SOCAR, and that is to be ready by October 1," Bayatly said.
AIOC will have to build a new pipeline linking the Caspian with Western oil markets to carry its main output.
--Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
